Without me, he would never have been released. Morgan le Fay detested him with all her heart and would never have relented. Yet his offense sprang more from carelessness than intentional wickedness. He had called her hair red. So it was, but that was not the proper way to mention it. Above a certain rank in society, red-haired people have auburn hair.

Think of it: of those forty-seven prisoners, five had lost all record of their names, crimes, and dates of imprisonment! One woman and four men, every one bowed, wrinkled, and patriarchal, with their minds extinguished. They had themselves forgotten such particulars long ago, or at least possessed only hazy guesses, nothing certain and nothing they could repeat twice alike. Successive priests, appointed to pray daily with the captives, remind them that God had placed them there for some wise reason, and instruct them that He delighted in patience, humility, and submission to oppression among the lower orders, retained traditions concerning these ruined old beings, but no more. Those traditions were of little assistance, for they dealt only with the duration of imprisonment, not with names or offenses. Even with tradition’s aid, all that could be established was that not one of the five had looked upon daylight in thirty-five years. How much longer they had lacked it nobody could guess. The king and queen knew nothing of the unfortunate creatures beyond their being heirlooms, assets inherited with the throne from the preceding firm. No account of their past had accompanied their persons; consequently the new owners considered them worthless and took no interest. I asked the queen:

“Then why on earth did you never release them?”

This question confounded her. She could not say why; the possibility had never entered her head. Unknowingly, she was anticipating the actual history of future prisoners in the Castle d’If. I understood now that, given her upbringing, these inherited captives were simply property, neither more nor less. And when we inherit property, throwing it away does not occur to us, even if we set no value upon it.

When I led my procession of human bats into the open air and the afternoon’s brilliant sunshine, they presented a sight indeed. First, in mercy to eyes so long spared the torment of light, I had blindfolded them. Skeletons, scarecrows, goblins, pitiable horrors, every one: the most legitimate offspring conceivable of Monarchy by the Grace of God and the Established Church.

Good heavens, she could talk. It would have been improper for me to mention the late hour or say that I was tired and terribly sleepy. I wished I had gone to bed when I had the chance. Now I had to endure it. Her bright chatter continued through the deep, ghostly silence of the sleeping castle. Eventually a distant sound rose from somewhere far beneath us, like a muffled scream. Its agony made my skin crawl. The queen stopped, her eyes bright with pleasure, and tilted her graceful head like a listening bird. The sound pierced the silence again.

“What is that?” I asked.

“A truly stubborn soul. He has endured it a long time—many hours now.”

“Endured what?”

“The rack. Come and see a delightful sight. If he refuses to reveal his secret now, you will see him torn apart.”

What a smooth, polished devil she was, so calm and peaceful while the muscles down my legs ached in sympathy with the man’s suffering. Armored guards carrying blazing torches led us through echoing corridors and down damp, dripping stone stairs. The place smelled of mold and centuries of trapped darkness. It was a long, cold, unsettling journey. The sorceress’s conversation, all about the prisoner and his crime, did nothing to make it shorter or pleasanter. An unnamed informer had accused him of killing a stag in the royal hunting grounds. I said:

“Anonymous evidence is hardly fair, Your Highness. The accused should be allowed to face his accuser.”

“I had not thought of that. It seemed unimportant. Even if I wished to, I could not arrange it. The accuser came masked at night, told the forester, and immediately left. The forester does not know who he is.”

“Then this unknown person was the only one who saw the stag killed?”

“No one saw the killing. But the stranger saw this bold scoundrel near where the stag lay. Out of proper loyalty, he reported him to the forester.”

“So the stranger was near the dead stag too? Couldn’t he have killed it himself? His loyalty, while wearing a mask, looks a little suspicious. But why torture the prisoner? What does Your Highness hope to gain?”

“He will not confess otherwise, and his soul would be lost. The law demands his life for the crime, and I will certainly make him pay it. But letting him die without confession or forgiveness would endanger my own soul.

But how was I, a bewildered country boy, to escape that astonishing inconsistency into which even the wisest and best men stumble daily?

“Perhaps every word is true,” I told Biddy, “but I admire her terribly.”

At that confession, in short, I rolled onto my face, gripped the hair at either side of my head, and pulled it hard. I knew all the while that my heart’s folly was so absurd and ill-directed that my face would have deserved its punishment had I hauled it up by the hair and dashed it against the stones for belonging to such a fool.

Biddy, the wisest girl imaginable, attempted no further argument. Her hand, reassuring though rough with work, rested upon each of mine in turn and gently freed them from my hair. Then she patted my shoulder softly to comfort me. With my face buried in my sleeve, I shed a few tears, just as I had in the brewery yard, dimly persuaded that somebody—or everybody; I could not say which—was treating me very badly.

“One thing makes me glad,” said Biddy. “You felt able to trust me with this, Pip. And another makes me glad too: of course you know you can count on me to keep your confidence, and to remain worthy of it at least in that respect. If your first teacher—dear me, what a poor teacher, and how much she needed teaching herself!—were teaching you now, she believes she knows the lesson she would give. But it would be difficult to learn, and you have passed beyond her, so it is useless now.” With a gentle sigh on my behalf, Biddy stood up from the bank and asked, her voice changing pleasantly and brightly, “Shall we go a little farther, or return home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, rising, slipping an arm around her neck, and kissing her, “I will always tell you everything.”

“Until you become a gentleman,” Biddy said.

“You know I never will, which means always. Not that I need tell you anything; you already know everything I know, as I said at home the other evening.”

“Ah!” Biddy whispered, looking away towards the ships. Then, with the same pleasant alteration in her tone, she repeated, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

I suggested we walk farther, and so we did. The summer afternoon softened into summer evening, and everything was very beautiful.
